Event Update

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, at approximately 8:30 PM CDT Friday, October 9, as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds near 105 mph. It has since weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and moved inland through Alabama into Tennessee.


The hurricane threat along the northern Gulf Coast has ended, but response and recovery are underway across communities affected by damaging winds, power outages, flooding, debris, and damage to homes, churches, and community facilities.


Serve Source is connecting churches, disaster-response ministries, and local leaders as verified needs become clear. Visit the response map to follow partner activity, share available resources, request help, and identify coordinated opportunities to serve. Everyone can do something—pray, give, share resources, or join a verified response effort.

Current Situation

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on October 9 as a Category 2 hurricane. The National Hurricane Center discontinued advisories on October 10 after Isaias weakened to a post-tropical cyclone over Alabama.


This is now a recovery event. The most immediate concerns are damaged homes, fallen trees, large debris volumes, road and utility hazards, household needs, and helping affected communities begin the long path toward recovery.

Recovery-Phase Hazards

  • Localized flooding, standing water, and hazardous road conditions
  • Downed trees, damaged structures, and blocked access routes
  • Downed or damaged power lines; treat all lines as energized
  • Scattered power outages and utility-restoration activity
  • Lingering rain and gusty winds across portions of Tennessee and the southern Appalachians
  • Dangerous coastal conditions may continue in some areas; follow local beach and emergency-management guidance

Residents should continue to follow instructions from local emergency management and the National Weather Service. Do not drive through floodwater, around barricades, or into areas with downed lines or unstable trees.

Areas of Initial Response Focus

Serve Source is monitoring verified impacts and partner activity across:

  • Florida Panhandle: Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, Walton, Bay, Holmes, and Washington Counties
  • Alabama: Baldwin, Mobile, Escambia, Conecuh, Covington, and other affected inland communities
  • Coastal Mississippi and southeastern Louisiana: continuing local monitoring for rain, coastal, and recovery-related impacts
  • Tennessee and the southern Appalachians: lingering rain and wind impacts as the post-tropical system moves northeast

This list reflects the areas of greatest expected or reported impact and may change as local damage assessments continue.

Partner Preparedness & Coordination

Serve Source has moved from storm monitoring to assessment and response coordination.


Partners shown on the Serve Source response map are reporting activities that may include:

  • Damage assessments and verified-needs reporting
  • Emergency meals, food distribution, water, and essential supplies
  • Resource and donation coordination
  • Tree and debris removal
  • Roof tarping and temporary weatherproofing
  • Flood cleanup and muck-out assistance where needed
  • Mobile shower, laundry, and volunteer-support services
  • Church, volunteer, and housing coordination


Churches and response organizations are encouraged to:

  • Update their Serve Source profile and response capabilities.
  • Submit verified local needs, damage reports, and available resources.
  • Coordinate with local emergency management before opening facilities or receiving volunteers.
  • Use the response map to connect with churches and organizations already serving nearby.
  • Avoid self-deployment. Wait for a verified request, local invitation, or coordinated deployment opportunity.
  • Share prayer needs and encourage affected leaders through the Serve Source event page.
  • If your church has been affected, needs assistance, has available resources, or is ready to serve, please update the Hurricane Isaias Active Event page so partners can respond in coordination.

Recovery is underway across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama. State, local, nonprofit, and faith-based partners are supporting feeding, supply distribution, damage assessment, debris removal, roof tarping, and survivor referrals. Florida has operated distribution points in impacted Panhandle counties, while local recovery coordination continues to expand. Executive Office of the Governor

Need Cleanup Help?

Residents in Escambia and Santa Rosa Counties who need help with storm cleanup can contact Crisis Cleanup to be connected with volunteer organizations that may be able to assist.

  • Roof tarping
  • Fallen-tree removal
  • Debris cleanup
  • Mucking out flooded homes
  • Other storm-cleanup needs


Call Crisis Cleanup: 1-800-451-1954

BRACE is coordinating with national disaster-relief organizations, local partners, and Long-Term Recovery Groups to help connect residents with available assistance. Assistance is dependent on volunteer capacity, safety conditions, and the needs reported.

Start Here: Safety, Evacuation & Immediate Help

  • If there is an immediate threat to life, call 911.
  • Do not drive through flooded roads, standing water, or around barricades.
  • Stay clear of downed power lines, damaged buildings, and unstable trees.
  • Check official local road conditions before traveling.
  • If your home or church has sustained damage, document conditions safely with photos and report verified needs through Serve Source.
  • For shelter information, food, housing, utility assistance, and other community support, contact 211 or your county/parish emergency-management office.
  • Do not self-deploy. Wait for a confirmed request and a coordinated assignment before entering affected communities.



Multi-Agency Resource Centers (MARC)

Floridians impacted by disasters can visit local MARC's to:

  • Request assistance for individuals, families & businesses from nonprofit & state partners for food, water, housing, recovery services & more
  • Meet with representatives from state agencies to inquire about storm recovery resources & services from storm clean-up to emotional support

*Bring identification, proof of residence, insurance information & other official documentation related to your disaster-related losses to ensure you receive the appropriate assistance.
